segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When Mike and Sara bought their house, they were in their 30s-- been renters all their lives. Not married, no kids yet, but heading there.

segments.speaker: Mike
segments.text: We had saved some money for a down payment, and we used all of that. So we had no money to furnish the house with.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: And we were two people who had been living like grad students, basically. So yeah, we moved in our futon, and we moved in our--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They had a little table that they got from Mike's dad's garage. Their chairs were these plastic stacking deck chairs-- the ones from Kmart. They had two desks. And that was about it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So most of the house was empty. Most of the rooms had nothing in them. And so on the weekends, they would go looking for furniture. At first, they tried yard sales. And then they learned about estate sales, barn sales. They live in Maine.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The thing that they wanted more than anything was to get a dining room table. If they had a dining room table, they could have friends over for dinner, and they really wanted that. But the problem was they never had enough money to win at these barn auctions. Somebody would always outbid them. And Mike says he was seeing a side of Sara he had never seen before.

segments.speaker: Mike
segments.text: She turned into an absolute different person at these barn auctions. They would hand her a paddle, and she would have to win, which is not good when you don't have any money.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: Yeah. You give me a paddle, and I'm not going to sit there with it on my lap the whole time. And so then I would get a little wound up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: After this one time when she spent hundreds of dollars that they did not have on something that looked from the back of the room where they were sitting like it was kind of a table but did not actually turn out to be a table, the two of them decided, OK, no more barn auctions. But Sara was not done.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: Well, then I discovered this little thing called eBay.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And this is like 1998, 1999. EBay is really new. They had just gone public. People like Sara are calling on dial-up modems. And Sara said that the first thing that she did when she got onto eBay was enter "dining room table" into the search box.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: And then I was amazed because suddenly there were all these pictures of tables, and you can just get them. Today it seems kind of old hat, but back then it really was exciting.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So at first, bidding on eBay was a lot like the barn auctions. Sara would bid on some piece of furniture and then ultimately did not have enough money to win. But she says that she was able to get a nice side table for $20. That gave her hope. And then one day--

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: The listing was "round walnut table and two chairs." And I clicked on it, and the starting bid was like $10, but then the shipping was really low.

segments.speaker: Mike
segments.text: I remember seeing a picture of it. It was kind of fancier than something we might normally go for, and the chairs looked great. It looked like what grown-up people would put in their house. Like, if we can put that table in here, that's it, that's the beginning. You could kind of see your kids sitting around that table someday.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So there's a brief bidding war, and Sara wins the table. She remembers it costing $20, Mike remembers it as $40. But the moment she won, that she's totally clear on.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: Are you kidding? On that front, I was elated. That felt great. It just felt like, wow, I could furnish our whole house for $400.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: I felt like suddenly, oh, we've been looking in the wrong places. We'd been going to these barn auctions, but people already know about that. But nobody knows about eBay yet. So yeah, I was really fired up about it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So a couple days pass. And one day Sara goes out to the mailbox, and there's a package. It's a box, like, half the size of a toaster.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: I was sort of like, oh, what's this? I brought it inside, and I came into the kitchen, and I opened up the box. And there was my walnut table and two chairs. And it was just as beautiful as it had been in the picture, but it was about 2 and 1/2 inches high. But it had the little velvet cushions, and it had a crocheted top on it. And it was from some guy in Maryland who makes doll furniture.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: And I sat and I stared at it, dumbfounded for so long, trying to decide how I felt. That was the first thing when I was staring at the doll table. It was one of those do I laugh or do I cry moments. And then I do remember getting back on eBay and realizing that when you put in a general search term, there are still categories. Because I went and found the listing, and it was under doll furniture.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Next, she showed it to Mike. And Mike says that when she showed him the toy table, at first he couldn't even understand what it was that he was looking at. His brain could not process the information-- like, what is this?

segments.speaker: Mike
segments.text: But then we were like, OK. That's fine. So we set it up in the dining room. So we had this big empty house and this tiny doll table with doll chairs set up in the dining room. And our friends started buying us little doll dishes and glasses.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So it was a perfect transaction except for that one thing.

segments.speaker: Mike
segments.text: Yeah. Until the cardboard box arrived.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: I do remember wanting Mike to see what a beautiful table it was, even if it was the wrong size. Like, that did matter. It was a nice table.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: And I remember when our friends came over and they would all mock me, it really was important to me that they saw-- I mean, it was a beautiful-- the guy who made it is an artist. I'm going to give him that. And it was walnut, and it was hand-carved, and it had a nice little rim around it. And it was a miniature version of exactly what I wanted.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, today on our radio program, "Except For That One Thing," we have stories today where everything is just like you would dream, just like you would wish for, except for one pesky detail, one flaw. And the people involved, they have to decide if they can live with that flaw, that one problem in how things worked out, or if they cannot live with it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's what growing up is about, right? Living with things not being absolutely perfect. Am I just talking for myself here? I hope not. OK. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 1, Run On Sentence. So lots of us have things about ourselves that we keep to ourselves that we assume people would see us differently if they knew about. And Mike Anderson had something like that, one thing about him in particular that he kept a secret, until one day it came out. Jessica Lussenhop explains.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: Mike Anderson was 36 years old, married, a suburban father of four. He owned a contracting business and built his family's modest, three-bedroom house in St. Louis from the ground up. He volunteered at church on the weekends and coached his son's football team. That changed last July. He was at home alone with his two-year-old daughter while his wife was away on a business trip.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: I was sleeping. I was awoken. It was about 6 o'clock in the morning, woken by knocking at the door. And it was unusual knocking. It was the consistent knocking, the hard knocking. So I knew something was going on.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: So I just stood at the top of the stairs for a moment. And finally I said, who is it? I'm in my boxers. And they said, marshals. Open it up, or it's coming down. Open up the door.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: As soon as I opened up the door, it was a small army. I mean, it was about eight of them. They had the shields. They had the helmets. They had the AR-15 style machine looking guns.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: And they had the street blocked off. And I said, hey, man, you got the wrong person. And he just looked at me. He said, no, you're the right person.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: The officer handcuffed him and asked, do you remember 13 years ago?

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: I broke out in a sweat. They had to sit me down. And the only thing I could think about, what's my wife going to say? What's she going to think?

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: I called her. And as soon as I called her, she was crying, what's going on? And I told her what was going on. I said, baby, this is from 13 years ago.

segments.speaker: Laqonna Anderson
segments.text: I'm freaking out-- I mean, screaming, crying.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: This is Mike's wife, LaQonna. They've been married for six years.

segments.speaker: Laqonna Anderson
segments.text: I can hear the marshals in the background telling him he has to go. So he told me he loved me, and that was it.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: And when you heard "something from 13 years ago," did you understand what that meant at all? Or what were you thinking?

segments.speaker: Laqonna Anderson
segments.text: I didn't understand what it meant until the next day, when we had a talk with the attorney. Then I just passed out. Hit my head on the concrete.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: Here's what LaQonna learned. In 1999, Mike was arrested for armed robbery but never served his time because of what amounted to a clerical error. He was 22 years old when he and a friend held up a Burger King manager making a night deposit at a bank.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: This wasn't a case of mistaken identity or wrongful conviction. Mike was there. Although his attorney instructed him not to discuss the details of the crime with me, Mike says he got caught up with the wrong crowd that night. Until then, he had no prior convictions and worked a full time job at AT&T.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: In court, Mike testified that the robbery wasn't his idea and that the gun his friend was holding was just a BB gun. The police never actually recovered any weapons, but Mike was convicted of armed criminal action and robbery. The judge sentenced him to 13 years in prison. Mike filed a series of appeals, but in the end, the courts decided, nope. He had to serve his sentence. At the time, Mike was out on bail.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: And here, something strange happened. At this point, Mike's bail should've been revoked, and he should have been arrested and taken to prison. But a warrant was never issued for that. Mike's attorney and the prosecutor appeared before a judge. Mike wasn't actually there himself.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: From what I understand, the judge asked, where is Mr. Anderson? My attorney handed her the briefs and told her Mr. Anderson is currently out on bond. But the prosecuting attorney at that time hopped up and said, no, he's not out on bond. I checked, my office checked, he's currently in prison. And so that was it.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: It was the prosecutor who told the judge that Mike was in custody, even though he wasn't, he was at home. Mike's attorney didn't say anything because he hadn't actually talked to Mike in a few days, and he thought maybe he really was back in prison-- until he talked to Mike on the phone.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: He was shocked. He said, you aren't in jail? I said, no, I'm not. And so I was like, what are we supposed to do? Am I supposed to turn myself in?

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: And it was just like, well, at this time, it's a mistake. They'll figure out their mistake. He says, temporary-- expect to be picked up. They're going to pick you up.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: It wasn't unusual for it to take a couple of weeks for a warrant to get issued, but months then years passed. No one ever came and picked up Mike.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: Mike says he never really considered turning himself in. He figured they'd either come for him or they wouldn't. And if they didn't, OK. That was God's plan for him. His lawyer was vague about what he should do next. He left it up to Mike.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: But after the arrest, the trial, the months he spent in prison before bonding out, Mike decided to turn his life around. He went back to school and became a master carpenter. He got married and became a family man who checked homework and got his kids ready for bed every night. Mike never had another run-in with the law.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: Did you feel like a fugitive during that time?

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: No. I never felt like a fugitive. Because a fugitive is someone that's running from the law. I never ran from the law. I was there.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: I registered my business through the state with a Social Security number, address, everything. I'm four streets over from the address that they had on file. I built a house over there. So there was never any running or strategy of, hey, I don't want to go here because there's going to be authorities. No, I lived a normal life.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: Did you feel relaxed right away? What was it like to sort of acclimate to this feeling that you're out and you may get to stay out?

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: It was 13 years of somewhat relief. But was it always in the back of my mind? Of course it was always in the back of my mind. Is that day coming any day now?

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: So like, you get pulled over for a traffic ticket. You run a red light, run a stop sign, or you didn't come into a complete stop. And they're running your information, and your heart's beating fast, like, man, are they going to know?

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: And they come back, hey, Mr. Anderson. Hey, get your taillight fixed. Get your tags renewed. And that was it. And I was just like, wow. What's going on?

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: In the end, the only reason that the Missouri Department of Corrections realized Mike was missing was because they were preparing to release him from prison. I called the Department of Corrections, the county's warrant officers, the original court where this happened, Missouri's Attorney General, and the state supreme court, and no one would say anything about how there was a record claiming that Mike was one of their inmates when he was, in fact, free.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: Meanwhile, Mike and his wife still have not had a frank conversation about all this either. They haven't discussed the fact that Mike knew all those years that he might someday go back to prison but never told her.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: Do you feel any sense of anger or wish that he had told you this earlier on?

segments.speaker: Laqonna Anderson
segments.text: I mean, that question arose in my head, just like, why he didn't tell me. I can't get mad at him because I understand why he hid it from me. He just wanted to protect me. So he didn't want to put too much on me that I couldn't handle. And that's just the type of person Mike is, too. He'll try to juggle everything by himself.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: It feels a little strange that you guys haven't had that conversation.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: It's uncomfortable for me because I'm always embarrassed about it. That's not who I am now. It's not who I'll ever be. I just want to forget.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: When I first visited Mike in November, he had to stay in his cell for about 22 hours a day in a huge penitentiary called Fulton Reception and Diagnostic, a gray building planted in the middle of farmland about two hours west of St. Louis. Usually clean cut, Mike had several months worth of beard on his chin.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: August, the kids went to school, their first day of school. Missed that. September, missed me and my wife's anniversary on the 26th. November, my son turned seven on the 5th, and my daughter turned 11 on the 10th. I missed a lot-- missed a lot.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: 13 years without going to prison did exactly what you'd hope 13 years in prison will do for a person. Mike reformed, became a model citizen. Which raises the question, do we want to send him to prison?

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: It'll cost the state of Missouri about $20,000 a year to house and feed him. And if Mike's no longer a danger to society, what's the point of having him sit in a cell when he could be out working, paying taxes, and raising his kids? Tim Lohmar is the prosecuting attorney in St. Charles County, where Mike was sentenced-- although he's not the one who jumped up in court and said Mike was in prison. That prosecutor has passed away.

segments.speaker: Tim Lohmar
segments.text: It still baffles me how this could have happened. But I think the state's interests are that this sentence has to be served.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: So he's had this life. He's had children, started a small business. hasn't had any run-ins with the law. Some people would say that he's been rehabilitated. He shouldn't have to serve the sentence because it took so long.

segments.speaker: Tim Lohmar
segments.text: Well, I can't say that that's not a reasonable thing for those people to think, especially his family, people who are close to him. Anybody who doesn't have sympathy for Mr. Anderson I think is not being genuine. It's a horrible tragedy for he and his family. So whether that spurs somebody at a higher pay grade than me to figure out a better way to do this, I don't know. You open Pandora's box.

segments.speaker: Tim Lohmar
segments.text: If our system allowed for people to somehow-- whether it was their doing or somebody else's doing-- to delay their incarceration to see if they can rehabilitate and become a productive member of society, become a family man, I don't know how we would do that. I don't know where you stop. Where do you draw the line? That's not a precedent that I feel that we can set.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: Mike's family hired a lawyer who's filed a brief arguing that when the state forgot about Mike for 13 years, they violated his constitutional right to due process, or speedy punishment, that now suddenly taking Mike away from his life because of the state's, quote, "utter and complete failure to act defines cruelty," end quote. If that fails, Mike can petition Missouri governor Jay Nixon for clemency. He's only granted that once.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: Then there's the victim from the robbery. You'd think if anyone would have an opinion about whether Mike should serve his time or not, it would be him.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: I hope someday that man can forgive me for what I was a part of. So I've always wanted to someway, somehow, reach out to him, but I always feared that it would be an intrusion. All I can do is just-- I'm sorry. I should have never been there that night.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: I first reported this story last summer for the St. Louis Riverfront Times. At that time, I couldn't find the victim. But then, right after my article published, he found me. His name is Dennis.

segments.speaker: Dennis
segments.text: I was sitting there back at work, eating my lunch and reading this magazine. Something about, oh, the guy was a Burger King manager at a night shift, and he got robbed out in St. Charles. And that's when I was like, wow, man, this is really trippy. That almost sounds like something that happened to me. And then when I got on down farther, then I was like, crap, they are talking about me.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: When he first contacted me, Dennis sent me an email saying, I was that victim. Why don't you talk to me, and I'll tell you how bad it screwed up my life. When we finally met, Dennis told me that getting robbed at gunpoint left him deeply paranoid. He even moved a few times, thinking the robbers might come looking for him to keep him from testifying.

segments.speaker: Dennis
segments.text: It started kind of getting to me a little bit, to where I wasn't sleeping at nights. And it kind of just escalated from there. I didn't want to be there at work no more, refused to take any money back to the bank, not at nighttime, anyway. I just didn't trust anybody, didn't want to do anything, didn't want to be anywhere. I just pretty much wanted to just be by myself.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: Dennis said he had problems in his life before the robbery-- with his marriage, with drinking. But he says after, they got worse. His marriage fell apart. And so when Dennis found out that Mike never served his sentence, he got pretty angry.

segments.speaker: Dennis
segments.text: But then the more I thought about it, it was like, what you're doing to him is not right. He wasn't out robbing other people, doing this, that, and the other. He seemed to have gotten his life together.

segments.speaker: Dennis
segments.text: You've got to give the guy a little bit of slack. I mean, yeah, he screwed up when he was little. But the law dropped the ball. The law ought to drop it completely. They need to leave the man alone.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: When you tell people that that's how you feel about it, does it surprise them?

segments.speaker: Dennis
segments.text: It's the weirdest thing. As I was sitting downstairs rereading that article one day for my daughter, she goes, Dad, we read this in school the other day. I was like, oh yeah? I said, oh.

segments.speaker: Dennis
segments.text: But at the time, she didn't know it was me. Because I just never talk about it. She said that she didn't think it was right, what they're doing to him now. And pretty much her whole class agreed with her.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: Then Dennis told her that he was the Burger King manager in that article and that he felt the same way she did. Two days after that conversation, I went back to the prison to talk to Mike. I told him what Dennis and his daughter said, that the state should let him go. He was overwhelmed.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: Wow, that's-- all I can say is praise, God. Thank God for that. And I don't know what to say. (CHOKING UP) I don't.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: He told me he was really sorry to be bothering Dennis by reminding him of the past.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: I appreciate him. I never want him to ever be-- this brought back to him. That's my fault. I appreciate him for that-- his daughter and the class. His daughter could be affected by that, you know? That's not something that I ever-- that's never my intent, and I don't want that.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: Mike is afraid of falling into the daily routines of prison. So aside from his church group, he doesn't interact much with the other inmates. He won't do things like watch TV with them or play cards. He also doesn't like writing his family letters.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: I try not to write anybody because I don't want to get used to this. I don't want my wife coming up here to visit me. She wanted to come up here the 1st of this month, and I said, no, don't do it.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: For eight years, we've never been apart. And I don't want her getting this image of me. I don't want anybody thinking this is who I am.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: If you could go back, would you turn yourself in at 22?

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: If I would have known this, yes. Yes. If it would have been something-- oh, definitely. Like I said, I would have rather done it then. I was 22, 23 at the time, didn't have any children, didn't have a wife, didn't have a mortgage, didn't have a car payment. The hurt would have been less then.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: No one, financially or physically, depended on me. It's almost like I feel like I've abandoned my job as a man and as a father. Because my mom, my wife, my kids, they're doing the same time I'm doing.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: As it stands now, Mike's sentence will keep him in until 2026. He'll be nearly 50 when he gets out. His two-year-old will just be starting high school. Accepting all that, it's just too crushing to consider.

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: I have to look at it like, no matter what, God's got me. I wake up every time the doors pop. Every time the intercom comes on, every time my name is called, I feel it's my time. I'm going home.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: How long do you think you can kind of keep up that mindset?

segments.speaker: Mike Anderson
segments.text: I'm going to keep up that mindset till the day I walk out of here. I have to. I can't sit here and think that I'll be here for 13 years. There's no way. Everything that I've been allowed to do that I've accomplished. It seems like it would be all for nothing.

segments.speaker: Jessica Lussenhop
segments.text: In November, Mike and his wife both expected he'd be home for Christmas. Now she just assures herself it'll be very soon. They talk on the phone almost every day. But they both told me they figure they'll finally discuss Mike's original crime, and the fact he kept it from her all those years, face-to-face, once this is all over, once he gets home.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jessica Lussenhop, she's the managing editor at the Riverfront Times in St. Louis. Since we first broadcast that story a year ago, a lot has changed for Mike Anderson and his family.

segments.speaker: News Anchor
segments.text: Four little children are back in the arms of their father tonight. They haven't seen him since US Marshals came to take him back to prison last July.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's right. Mike Anderson was released this past May when a judge decided keeping him in prison was a waste of taxpayer money and that, quote, "it would unnecessarily punish an obviously rehabilitated man." Then six months after being released, Mike was back behind bars.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He was leaving a restaurant, 1:00 in the morning. And he was stopped by police, identified as a man who had just stolen a purse. Mike Anderson said he was innocent. He was nowhere near the scene of the crime when the crime happened.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He'd said he'd been in the restaurant with his wife at a party his employer was throwing. He was charged with felony, second degree robbery. Then three months after being arrested, new evidence emerged. Surveillance footage proved Mike had been telling the truth all along. Here's Circuit Attorney Jennifer Joyce.

segments.speaker: Jennifer Joyce
segments.text: My apologies to Mr. Anderson. Mr. Anderson did not commit this crime.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so two times, Mike Anderson became a free man. Coming up after the break, a date that is close, so close to being perfect, except for one thing. That's in a minute, from Chicago Public Radio, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program, "Except For That One Thing." Stories where everything is perfect, except for one inconvenient detail.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We have arrived at Act 2 of our program. Act 2, Not Okay Cupid. This is a piece of fiction by BJ Novak-- a piece of fiction that, with his help, we've turned into a little radio drama. It takes place at a restaurant. Hold on, let me cue restaurant sound, please.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [CHATTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There we go. OK. Here's our story.

segments.speaker: Julie
segments.text: OK. Now, you, sir.

segments.speaker: Bj Novak
segments.text: Julie finished the second-to-last half sip of her third complicated cocktail.

segments.speaker: Julie's Date
segments.text: Yes?

segments.speaker: Julie
segments.text: You, sir. Now, I am-- OK. [LAUGHS] I feel like we've only talked about me, but I don't know anything about you, other than that you're very charming, and well, very cute, of course. Don't let that go to your head. Shouldn't have said that. Shouldn't have said that.

segments.speaker: Julie's Date
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Julie
segments.text: OK. If this is my-- [LAUGHS] OK. What do you do?

segments.speaker: Julie's Date
segments.text: What do I do? You mean, what is my job?

segments.speaker: Julie
segments.text: Sorry. I hate that question, too. It's like, is this a date or an interview, right?

segments.speaker: Bj Novak
segments.text: He finished his bite of sauce-soaked broccolini and answered.

segments.speaker: Julie's Date
segments.text: [INAUDIBLE] lord.

segments.speaker: Julie
segments.text: Hm? All I heard was "lord."

segments.speaker: Julie's Date
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: BJ Novak, that story, "Julie and the Warlord," is from his book of short stories called One More Thing-- Stories and Other Stories . Our amazing actors-- Alison Brie played Julie. Tunde Adebimpe was the warlord.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 3, Hungry Hungry People. There was a period in the early 1900s in our country when meat was actually scarce because of huge waves of immigrants coming in. Plus, there was also a growing demand for us to export meat to other countries. And meat was scarce enough that the thinkers and journalists and politicians of the day didn't just call it a meat shortage. The problem was commonly referred to by this loftier, more zen-like name, the Meat Question.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jon Mooallem wrote a long story about this for The Atavist online. He says that there would be newspaper editorials about what are we going to do about the Meat Question. It pops up in congressional testimony on unrelated subjects. People will say, well, you know, it's just like the Meat Question. The question being, how are we going to raise enough meat for all the people here?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jon Mooallem talked to This American Life producer Alex Blumberg about all this. He said it wasn't like American industry wasn't trying to produce more meat.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: This is like Upton Sinclair, The Jungle era. So you have the industry just ramping up and trying to become as efficient as it can. But it's just not happening. It's just the supply was still being dwarfed by the demand. And--

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: No matter how many rats and human fingers they added, they just couldn't produce enough meat.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: Well, right. And people were actually a little bit worried. There were rumors that Germans were eating dogs and all this stuff. And could it happen here, too?

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: And in that way, it was also really an existential crisis for the country at the same time because literally, we had gone all the way west. People talk about the frontier being closed. There wasn't a sense that there was more to scoop up in America. Passenger pigeons and buffalo had been decimated. You had forests that had been overlogged and destroyed.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: And then suddenly, about 1900, 1910, this kind of regret started to seep into the culture where people were kind of looking around and wondering, well, what have we done? And what did that say about the country at the turn of the century if no one could come up with some innovative idea to kind of hit this problem head on and solve it?

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: OK. So there's the problem. It's a problem that's crying out for bold solutions. And low and behold, somebody comes forth with a bold solution.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: Right. It was a very bold solution. The solution was hippopotamuses.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Explain. Explain further. How are hippopotamuses going to fix the problem?

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: OK. It was really going to be cool. The problem basically is we don't have any more land. We've hit the Pacific Ocean. So what we need to do is look at land that right now looks completely worthless and find a way to extract the energy that's hidden in that land and turn it into meat.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: The swamps all along the Gulf Coast-- you can't have a cow trudging through a swamp, eating muddy water. It's not going to survive. You can't graze it there. But you could take a hippopotamus and put it in that landscape, and it would eat aquatic plants.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: So the hippopotamus was this-- today we'd call it a very disruptive technology. It was going to turn something that seemed worthless and leverage it into millions of tons of meat to solve this big crisis.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And there's two main sort of characters at the center of your story who were behind this-- Frederick Burnham and a man named Fritz Duquesne. And both of them have very sort of colorful back histories, but they both spent time in Africa, were sort of very, very talented outdoor guide, survival guide scouts.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: Yeah. Someone had called Burnham the most complete human being who ever lived, I guess you would say, like a shorthand.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And these guys were actually, you write-- for much of their lives, they were mortal enemies. For a large part of their lives, they were actually spies. They fought against each other. But they had actually come together at this point over this idea, the hippo idea. And then at a certain point, this idea, with their help, makes its way to Congress.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: Yeah. So a congressman named Robert Broussard from Louisiana-- his constituents called him Cousin Bob. He insisted he was cousins with half of the people in his district. And Broussard brought a bill to the Agriculture Committee of the House of Representatives to ask for $250,000 for the importation of useful animals, the hippopotamus being-- that was the example they felt ready to go ahead with, the common hippopotamus.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And Jon writes that everyone involved in this idea had their own motivations. For Congressman Bob Broussard, it was to solve a problem in his district-- the water hyacinth. It came to New Orleans during the World's Fair, which was also known as the World Industrial and Cotton Centennial, when a group of Japanese visitors had given a bunch of water hyacinths away as gifts.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: And the water hyacinth, basically, was a plague in the bayous of Louisiana. It was choking all these rivers and stopped shipping. Boats couldn't get through with cargo. Fish died because there was no oxygen left in the water.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: And there were all sorts of attempts to kill the flower, none of which worked. The US War Department was on the job, just even pouring oil all over the flower, hoping to kill it. So the idea was the hippos could be brought in, put in the rivers. They'd suck up all this aquatic vegetation. And so they'd literally ingest one problem and convert it into the solution for the other problem, which was the meat crisis.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Two birds.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: Exactly. As I say, it was a perversely elegant win-win, the hippopotamuses.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: It does. It makes a lot of sense.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Except that it's utterly ridiculous, right?

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: OK. Right, it's utterly ridiculous. But can you tell me why?

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Well, it's just-- hippopotamus is just a ridiculous thing.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: OK. So I don't disagree with what you're saying, but you're telling me why it sounds ridiculous. You're not telling me why it is ridiculous. And I'm not saying that it's not ridiculous. OK? I'm just saying that I can't yet locate exactly why it is ridiculous.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And actually, as you looked into it, there was a lot of reasons why this plan should actually work.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: And maybe not even why it would work, but there's a logic to it. I was surprised by how much logic there was to it. That was what drew me in.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And you can really see this logic on display in the congressional hearing about this idea. Back in 1910, testimony was heard for Broussard's bill, HR 23261, also known as the hippo bill. One of the main people called on to testify? Fred Burnham.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: Burnham did a really good job of making this sound normal. He made the point that, OK, what are the animals that Americans eat? Chickens, pigs, cows, sheep, lambs. None of those, really, are native to the US.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: They were all brought centuries before by people from other parts of the world. But they had been here so long that we took them for granted as American cuisine. Really, the only thing that was native was turkeys. And we only ate that once a year.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: So why did we suddenly stop feeling free enough to change the landscape that way? And so the idea of solving the Meat Question this way, this is sort of where the beautiful poetry of it is. It was this key that unlocked all these other feelings of optimism and ambition and sort of stick-to-itiveness that America wanted to feel again. Because it was a way of saying, we have the smarts and the courage to solve this in a bold way.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: What about, though, the other reaction, which is sort of like, yuck. That's disgusting. I'm not going to eat hippo meat. Yuck.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: Right. There was a lot of that. There was a kind of campaign to nudge people past that. You had this guy, WN Irwin, at the Department of Agriculture who was helping Burnham and Duquesne promote it. Apparently he had a supply of hippopotamus jerky that he offered to reporters here and there in his office.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: And I found this story in the Washington Post. He had actually given it to a Washington Post reporter as he showed the Washington Post reporter a photo of that very hippo being skinned in Africa by a crowd of men. And that reporter liked it. "Toughness is only skin deep," is what he wrote.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: So obviously, the state of Louisiana is not covered in hippo ranches. We don't have hippo bacon on the menus of fancy restaurants. So what happened? What got in the way of this vision?

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: Yeah. That's a really good question. What got in the way of this vision? Frankly, a lot of the problem was administrative. They're all writing letters to each other all summer, all three men, trying to get this new food supply society up and running, which was going to be a lobbying firm to promote the idea in the next session of Congress. And I said to my editor on the story, I said, I'm starting to get the impression that if they had had email, this might have actually happened.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: It's just so infuriating. Duquesne writes to Broussard and says, what can I do for you? But Broussard is in South America. And then when he comes back, he gets the flu. And so you have back and forth with his secretary.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: Or Burnham is traveling in Mexico and can't be reached. Or someone misses a letter. They never got the letter. So then they write back two weeks later, I never received your reply to my last letter. So it got really messy and sloppy.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: You tell this story at the very end of-- there's this scene at the very, very end of this piece that you wrote, where Frederick Burnham is now an older man. It's 1944.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: Yeah. 34 years after all this. At this point, he's a very distinguished man. He's become very wealthy. And he was preparing his papers for posterity at both Stanford and Yale. I guess that's how you know you've had an impressive life, when both Stanford and Yale libraries want your archives.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: And he finds this speech that he had given to a civic organization in Pasadena in 1910. And he reads over the speech. And there he is in 1910, 34 years earlier, making the case to the general public of why this is going to work, why it's necessary, and just urging these laypeople to understand that what he calls the complacent belief in the unending plenty of our natural wealth was now so totally false. It was so obvious that wasn't true anymore.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: But that here he was, humbly with this idea. He's assuring them. He's saying, the idea made sense. It makes sense. But it's going to require working against what he calls overwhelming difficulties and the loud guffaws of the ignorant to make it a reality.

segments.speaker: Jon Mooallem
segments.text: And here he is, he reads this over. And still, he takes a pen and he writes in this very shaky, kind of old-man hand, he writes, "The facts are still unrefuted." And he signs it "FRB, 1944." And then he sends it off to the archives, which is where I found it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jon Mooallem talking to Alex Blumberg, who these days you may have heard on the StartUp podcast. You can read Jon's full account of the American hippopotamus, including everything about the crazy rivalry between Fred Burnham and Fritz Duquesne that we were not able to get into, at theativist.com. It's also available on amazon.com as an ebook.

segments.text: Act 4, Start Me Up. When comedian Tig Notaro was in sixth grade, she took this music class, and it was the kind of class where they would talk about Beethoven and The Who. segments.text: It was so much fun. I just-- I loved it. I was a huge Beatles and Rolling Stones fan. And at the end of every class, the teacher would let one kid play their favorite song for the whole class to hear. And I always brought in Beatles and Rolling Stones albums.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: And the coolest kid in our entire school, JD-- of course-- he came up to me after school one day, and he said, if I bring in my dad's Rolling Stones album, will you tell me a cool song to play? I said, absolutely. No doubt.

segments.text: Act 5, Happy Accident. Etgar Keret always had a good relationship with his dad, except for one thing. This story is true. It all happens in Israel, where Etgar lives, and was read for us in English translation by actor Michael Chernus.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "30 years I'm a cabbie," the small guy sitting behind the wheel tells me. "30 years and not one accident." It's been almost an hour since I got into his taxi in Beersheba, and he hasn't stopped talking for a second.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: Under different circumstances, I would tell them him to shut up, but I don't have the energy for that today. Under different circumstances, I wouldn't shell out 350 shekels to take a taxi to Tel Aviv. I would take the train. But today I feel that I have to get home as early as I can.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: I spent last night at Ichilov Hospital with my wife. She had a miscarriage and was bleeding heavily. We thought it would be OK, till she passed out. It wasn't until we got to the emergency room that they told us that her life was in danger and gave her a blood transfusion.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: Three days before that, my dad's doctors told me and my parents that the cancer at the base of his tongue, which had been in remission for four years, was back. And the tumor was at such an advanced stage that the only way to fight it was to remove his tongue and larynx. The oncologist said she didn't recommend having the surgery, but my dad said that he was for it.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: The oncologist told him that the operation would leave him seriously handicapped, unable to speak or eat. "At my age," my dad said, "all I need are my heart and my eyes so I can enjoy watching my grandchildren grow."

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: When we left the room, the doctor whispered to me, "Try to talk to him." She clearly doesn't know my dad.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: The taxi driver repeats, for the 100th time, that in 30 years, he hasn't had a single accident and that all of a sudden, five days ago, his car kissed the bumper of the car in front of him, traveling at 20 kilometers per hour. When they stopped and checked, he saw that except for a scratch on the left side of the bumper, the other car hadn't really been damaged at all. He offered the other driver 200 shekels on the spot. But the driver insisted that they exchange insurance information.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: The next day, the driver, a Russian, asked him to come to a garage. And he and the owner, probably a friend of his, showed him a huge dent all the way on the other side of the car and said the damage was 2,000 shekels. The cab driver refused to pay, and now the other guy's insurance company was suing him. "Don't worry, it'll be OK," I tell him, in the hope that my words will make him stop talking for a minute.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "How will it be OK?" he complains. "They're going to screw me. Those bastards are going to squeeze the money out of me. You see how unfair it is? Five days I haven't slept. Do you get what I'm saying?"

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "Stop thinking about it," I suggest. "Try thinking about other things in your life, happy things."

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "I can't," the cab driver groans and grimaces. "I just can't."

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "Then stop talking to me about it," I say. "Keep on thinking and suffering, but just don't tell me about it anymore, OK?"

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "It's not the money," the taxi driver continues, "believe me. Yesterday I went with my son to the graves of the Sadikim. We bought blessings for 1,800 shekels, and I didn't mind paying. It's the injustice that gets me."

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "Shut up," I say, finally losing it. "Just shut up for a minute!"

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "What are you yelling for?" the cab driver asks, insulted. "I'm an old man. It's not nice."

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "I'm yelling because my father is going to die if they don't cut his tongue out of his mouth," I continue to yell. "I'm yelling because my wife is in the hospital after a miscarriage." The driver is silent for the first time since I got into his taxi. And now I'm suddenly the one who can't stop the stream of words.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "Let's make a deal," I say. "Get me to an ATM, and I'll take out 2,000 shekels and give it to you. In exchange, it'll be your father who has to have his tongue removed and your wife who's lying in a hospital bed getting a blood transfusion after a miscarriage."

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: The driver is still silent, and now so am I. I feel a little uncomfortable for having shouted at him but not uncomfortable enough to apologize. To avoid his eyes, I look out the window. We missed the exit to Tel Aviv. I tell him that politely-- or I shouted angrily, I don't recall anymore.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: He tells me not to worry. He doesn't really know the way, but in a minute, he'll find out. A few seconds later, he parks in the right lane of the highway after managing to convince another driver to stop. He starts to get out of the taxi to ask for directions to Tel Aviv.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "You'll kill us both," I tell him. "You can't stop here."

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "30 years I'm a cabbie," he tosses back at me as he gets out of the taxi. "30 years and not one accident."

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: Alone in the cab, I can feel the tears rising. I don't want to cry. I don't want to feel sorry for myself. I want to be positive like my dad. My wife is fine now, and we already have a wonderful son. My dad survived the Holocaust.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: That's not just the half-full glass, it's an overflowing one. I don't want to cry, not in this taxi, not next to this driver that I yelled at. The tears are welling up and will soon begin to flow.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: Suddenly I hear a crashing boom and the sound of windows breaking. The world around me shatters. A silver car veers across the next lane, completely smashed.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: The taxi moves too, but not on the ground. It floats above it, towards the concrete wall on the side of the road. After it hits, there's another bang. Another car must have hit the taxi.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: A second before the ambulance drives away, they load the taxi driver into it. Deep in my heart, I was hoping they'd send us in separate ambulances, but it just wasn't my day. The driver, looking revitalized and happy, lights a cigarette. The paramedic wears a yarmulke and tells me I was very lucky. An accident like that with no deaths is a miracle.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "The minute you're discharged from the hospital," he says, "you should run to the nearest synagogue and give thanks for still being alive." My cellphone rings. It's my dad. He's only calling to ask how my day at the university was and whether the little one is asleep yet.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: I tell him that the little one is sleeping and my day at the university was great. And Shira, my wife, is fine, too. She just stepped into the shower.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "What's that noise?" he asks.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "An ambulance siren," I tell him. I try to sound casual. "One just passed by on the street."

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: Once, five years ago when I was in Sicily with my wife and son, I called my dad to ask how he was. He said everything was fine. In the background, a voice on a loudspeaker was calling a Dr. Shulman to the operating room.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "Where are you?" I asked.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "In the supermarket," my dad said without a moment's hesitation. "They're announcing on the loudspeaker that someone lost her purse." He sounded so convincing when he said that, so confident and happy.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: "Why are you crying?" my dad asks now from the other side of the line.

segments.speaker: Michael Chernus
segments.text: I force myself to smile, hoping he can sense it, too. "It's nothing," I say as the ambulance stops next to the emergency ward and the paramedic slams the ambulance doors open. "Really, it's nothing."

segments.text: Michael Chernus, reading a story by Etgar Keret. Etgar's most recent book is Suddenly a Knock on the Door.
